Where it began

Born in Choryasi, near Surat, on 11 October 1993, Hardik Pandya grew up in Vadodara. He and his brother Krunal, who has also played for India, learned the game at Kiran More's cricket academy there.

For a long time he bowled leg-spin. It was only at around 18 that the Baroda coach Sanath Kumar persuaded him to try bowling fast instead, which turned out to be sound advice. He has played for Baroda since 2013, and helped them win the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy in his first season.

The player

Pandya is a right-handed middle-order hitter and a lively fast-medium bowler, and most cricket followers know him from the white-ball game. His Test career was short but bright. He made his debut at Galle on 26 July 2017, and played 11 Tests in all between 2017 and 2018.

In those 11 Tests he made 532 runs at 31.29, with one hundred and four fifties, and took 17 wickets at 31.06. His best bowling was five for 28. Few players pack that much into so brief a taste of Test cricket.

What made him special

The high point came in the third Test of that first series, at Pallekele. He made 108 and became the first Indian to complete a Test hundred just before lunch. Along the way he hit 26 off a single over, at the time the most any Indian had taken from one over in a Test. It was his first hundred in international cricket of any kind.

If there is a regret for Test followers, it is simply that there were not more of these days. He has been in such demand in the shorter formats that the long game saw rather less of him than it would have liked.

Away from the middle

In white-ball cricket he has done a great deal. He was vice-captain when India won the 2024 T20 World Cup, and bowled the final over of the final. Afterwards he became the first Indian all-rounder to top the T20 International rankings, and he was the first fast-bowling all-rounder to reach 1,000 runs and 100 wickets in that format. In the IPL he led the Gujarat Titans to the title in 2022, their very first season, and he later went back to the Mumbai Indians as their captain.

And finally

Reaching a Test hundred in the last overs before lunch is a fine way to work up an appetite. The bowlers, one imagines, had rather less of one.
